criteria.name: Mission concept and rationale — What will it do, who are the users, why is it needed?
criteria.reasoning: Clear mission purpose, identified users (marine/conservation scientists), and strong rationale for Australia's GBR, supported by four literature citations. However, explicit mission goals, objectives and quantified requirements are not formally stated, keeping it at the lower end of Accomplished.

evidence.quote: A near-real-time relay to monitoring stations on the ground would allow marine and conservation scientists to more accurately predict and react to coral bleaching events.
Reef-monitoring satellites could also be used to report sea surface temperatures, thermal stress on coral, and bathymetry

criteria.name: Project plan — How you plan to complete the assignment, including either a Gantt chart or a timetable and information sources you plan to use
criteria.reasoning: A detailed Gantt chart with week-by-week tasks, deadlines and narrative tying tasks to the mission (launch, orbit, ground control, comms, end-of-life). Fits the mission narrative well, but no provision for contingencies/variations and no consolidated list of planned information sources.

evidence.quote: Project work will be divided into weeks via a Gantt Chart. Detailed task descriptions can be found on the next page.
In addition to my own research, the syllabus work on astrodynamics will help me to understand and design an optimal mission.

criteria.name: Preliminary progress — Technical content and evidence of sufficient work done to date
criteria.reasoning: Progress consists of literature research and completing four STK tutorials, but no preliminary results, calculations, or STK outputs are presented or interpreted. The stated orbit concept contains a fundamental technical error (see technical issues), indicating early-stage understanding.

evidence.quote: I have read the brief of Asner's monitoring system in Hawaii, researched into how coral bleaching occurs and its severity, and also completed STK tutorials 1, 2, 3 & 4.
My current choice is a geostationary orbit at an altitude of 600 km, which keeps the satellite fixed above the reef at all times.

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: Clear logical structure with headings, well-written prose, consistent formatting, and a well-labelled, legible Gantt chart. References are cited in text and match listed URLs, though footnote-style URLs rather than a formal reference list slightly weaken scholarly presentation.

evidence.quote: Completed stages are gold. Incomplete stages are blue. Deadlines are indicated by red lines.

technical_issues.issue: A geostationary orbit requires ~35,786 km altitude; a 600 km orbit is LEO and cannot keep the satellite fixed above the reef. Also, GEO coverage of the whole GBR would have poor resolution for seafloor colour detection.
The 2017 bleaching statistic ('another 50 percent perished') likely misrepresents the source, which referred to northern/central sections, not the entire reef.

overall: Well-motivated, clearly written mission concept benefiting Australia with a detailed Gantt-chart plan and STK selection. Weakened by a fundamental orbit technical error, absence of preliminary results/calculations, and no contingency planning or consolidated source list.

feedback.summary: Your GBR monitoring satellite concept is well motivated, clearly written, and supported by literature, with a detailed week-by-week Gantt chart and STK tutorials completed. To reach higher levels, formally state mission goals, objectives and quantified requirements, correct the orbit error (GEO is ~35,786 km, not 600 km), add contingency planning and a consolidated source list, and present preliminary STK results with interpretation.
next_steps: Correct the orbit section: explain that geostationary orbit requires ~35,786 km altitude, and evaluate whether a LEO constellation or other orbit better suits GBR coverage and seafloor colour resolution
Add explicit, quantified mission goals, objectives and requirements (e.g. spatial resolution, revisit time, SST/bathymetry products) linking each to user needs
Extend the Gantt chart with contingency provisions for schedule variations, and compile a formal reference list of all planned information sources beyond the four URLs
Include preliminary technical outputs from STK (e.g. coverage simulations, orbit plots) with brief interpretation as evidence of progress
Verify statistics against sources: the 2017 bleaching figure referred to northern/central reef sections, not the entire reef

criteria.C1: Your Mission Concept & Rationale clearly explains the GBR monitoring purpose, identifies marine and conservation scientists as users, and cites four sources — a strong Accomplished performance. To move higher in this band, formally state mission goals, objectives and quantified requirements, and double-check statistics (the 2017 bleaching figure applied to northern/central sections, not the whole reef).
criteria.C2: Your Gantt chart with weekly tasks and deadlines, tied to the mission narrative (launch, orbit, ground control, comms, end-of-life), is a solid Adequate-level plan. The next level requires provision for project variations and contingencies, plus a consolidated, referenced list of planned information sources beyond the four URLs cited in the concept section.
criteria.C3: Your literature research and completion of STK tutorials 1–4 show genuine effort, but no preliminary results, calculations or STK outputs are presented or interpreted, keeping you at Adequate. Note the orbit error: a geostationary orbit requires ~35,786 km, not 600 km. Presenting early STK coverage or orbit results with brief interpretation would demonstrate Accomplished-level progress.
criteria.C4: Your report is clearly structured, well written, and consistently formatted, with a well-labelled Gantt chart — a strong Accomplished performance. To strengthen further, replace footnote-style URLs with a formal reference list so in-text citations and the reference list match completely, as expected at the top of this band.
